In the bill I find one or two anomalies, one in particular. I refer to the maximum, compensation that may be awarded an employee with fifteen years or more of service. I am inclined to believe some hardship may result there. I realize that the measure as it stands has been approved by the standard railway organizations, yet I believe it possible that in its operation it may work some injustice. After a person has given fifteen or twenty years of service to a railway he is likely to be somewhere around fifty-five years of age. He may find his job done away with by some process of cooperation. He thereby loses his right to pension and is entitled to only five years' compensation under this measure. To-day men fifty-five years of age find it the most difficult thing in the world to secure new avenues of employment; so that in the case of the long-term employees I think some provision might have been made for extra compensation, because after all they have given a much greater part of their lifetime to the building up of the railway service and the betterment of the community than the man who has been only four or five years in the railway service yet who receives in proportion exactly the same compensation. I see the minister shake his head. I believe a man receives compensation for about thirty per cent of the time he has been with the railway, does he not?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: No. The second man receives the same percentage of compensation for a shorter period. A man who has been with the railway for two years receives compensation for six months.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: He gets the same percentage in proportion. If a man has been with the railway for fifteen years he is given compensation for five years which is equal to one third of the time he has been with the railway. A man who has been employed for six years would receive compensation for two years.

The ease of a man in the
service for fifteen years being thrown out of employment is not likely to arise under cooperative measures, because he is protected by the seniority rules. He is usually demoted, while the man let out is the man with four or five years of seniority. Those are the people who bear the brunt of it.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That is perfectly correct
so far as it goes, but unfortunately I have seen many men with fifteen and twenty years of service who have been let out of railway employment during the last few years.

speechtext: Oh, no.

I have seen and spoken to
them, and I am afraid there may be quite a number of such cases. However, in a general way I wish to give approval to the measure, because it recognizes the principle that a man who loses his job is just as much entitled to compensation as is the man who has money invested in one of these corporations.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I find
myself perfectly in accord with the principles of this bill, which I believe are very sound. The day has long gone when the only interest of an employee in the corporation which employs him, particularly if it is a public utility, is in his pay envelope. Over a period of years he has made a contribution to the success of that undertaking which may be difficult to estimate and impossible accurately to measure, but which deserves some recognition. This bill embodies a principle which from time to time I have advocated in discussing amalgamation, unification or cooperation of the railways. The Railway Act, which is chapter 179 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, provides by section 179:
179. The company shall not, at any time, make any change, alteration or deviation in the railway, or any portion thereof, until the provisions of the last preceding section are fully complied with nor remove, close, or abandon any station, or divisional point nor create a new divisional point which would involve the removal of employees, without leave of the board; and where any such change is made the company shall compensate its employees as the board deems proper for any financial loss caused to them by change of residence necessitated thereby.
I am familiar with the history of the last part of that section. It will be found first enacted in the statutes of 1913, and the amendment arose out of the following circumstances. The Grand Trunk Railway proposed to change the divisional point at Brockville to a point some twelve or fifteen miles east. Of course the municipality was very much exercised and the railway employees were disturbed. At that time I happened to occupy a position in the municipality which brought me in close touch with those conditions.

speechtext: And the Minister of Railways happened to be from Brockville.

No, not after 1911. That
was after the election.

speechtext: I thought it was Doctor Reid.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
No,, it was the Hon. Frank Cochrane, who was minister of railways in the government of Sir Robert Borden. The community was very much disturbed by the proposed change-and well it might be

Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act
Here were three or four hundred employees drawing a large monthly payroll, which was distributed and spent in tire municipality. These men were fine citizens who had lived in the community for many years and had made their contribution to its churches and to its municipal, social and business life. If action had been taken on the basis then proposed, the result would have been the removal of these men and their families from one community to another. Not only that, but they were to be located at a point where probably a new town would have to be built to accommodate them, so that notwithstanding their contribution to the building up of the public utilities and general advantages of a well-established town, they would have had to start all over again and go through a pioneering period. A memorial which I assisted in drafting was prepared, representations were made to the government, and as a result this provision for compensation in the event of the removal of a terminal was introduced.
I believe that is the germ of the bill now before us. Employees are entitled to consideration in circumstances of the kind, and the bill proposes a measure of justice for them. In the instance I have described the removal of the men would have involved heavy loss to the municipality. The properties they had acquired over a period of years would have been depreciated in value; in fact it would have been difficult for them to realize even half the value. At that time the recognition of the principle I have described was sound, and I believe recognition of the same principle is equally sound to-day. I am pleased that it is being embodied in legislation and I am sure it will assist in bringing about that measure of cooperation which we desire and which in the public interest is necessary. After all, I believe that is what will make for permanent and steady, rather than part time, employment of railway men.
The only suggestion I would make is that possibly the bill should provide for a threeway contribution. These changes are made in the interests of the public. When a grade crossing is eliminated the legislation provides for joint contributions. It appears to me the burden upon the railway companies and upon all parties concerned might be lightened by a three-way contribution-from each of the railways concerned, and from the federal treasury.
If the scale of compensation has been accepted or generally approved by the employees, it seems to me that scale ought to be satisfactory to all concerned. The measure embodies a just principle and a 71492-290J
measure of compensation to employees who, in the public interest-not on their own account or in the interests of the corporation they may have served for a long time- are deprived of their positions.
For these reasons, and for others so ably expressed by my leader, I heartily concur in the measure.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CANADIAN PACIFIC ACT, 1933 -COMPENSATION OF EMPLOYEES AFFECTED BY COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise to support in principle the measure sponsored by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). The explanatory note states the following:
The purpose of this bill is to provide for the payment of compensation by the employing company to railway employees who are deprived of employment or adversely affected by cooperative measures undertaken by the Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company pursuant to the provisions of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933.
I believe that a substantial measure of economy could be effected in connection with high interest rates now paid on railway issues, as well as in connection with the salaries of the high officials of both railways. We know, for example, that in the past it was common knowledge that certain high railway officials in Canada received fabulous salaries. It was also believed throughout the country that railway employees were receiving wages on a standard higher than that enjoyed by any other class of labour in Canada. From time to time, however, it has been shown definitely that that is not the case. As a matter of fact, so far as salaries are concerned the railway employees themselves have, from time to time, shown the way. I say further, in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway in the province of Nova Scotia, that the Dominion Atlantic railway was owned, completely equipped and well operated by an English company until it was gradually absorbed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company through stock control. If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have got themselves into financial difficulties, it is not the business of this parliament to pull them out. The railway has been an asset to Canada. The great development of our Canadian west was brought about by the influx of people in those splendid years which Canada was experiencing up until the great war of 1914, but from then on things started to go downward. To-day you have your great western country grid-ironed with railways. We in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have as our only railway asset, save for the Canadian Pacific running into St. John, the Intercolonial railway, and I for one, Mr. Speaker, intend so long as I am in this house to see to it, so far as I can, that every inch of that railway shall be protected for the people of the maritime provinces; that every employee of the railway shall continue to be employed under the terms of the agreements which have been entered into. If they want to have this cooperation and not amalgamation, in reference to railways which are not protected, I sound a note of warning that the only action on the part of the provinces would be to make application to the courts for an injunction to

restrain any action which would result in the destruction or removal or closing down of railways or railway stations or the dismissal of railway employees.
This bill is to my mind the thin end of the wedge in relation to Canada's railway transportation system. Action will not stop there; it is going to grow and develop to such an extent that, if parliament does not take the whip hand, the country will find itself in anything but a happy position. In the Canadian west the farmers have received millions of dollars in relation to grain, to the land situation, and to irrigation schemes. Let us do the best we can to assist them in every way, but let us not, while we are building up one class of people by the direct vote of funds in this parliament, pull down another class by the destruction of railways and the dismissal of railway employees. The control of thirty-five or thirty-six thousand miles of railway is a tremendous responsibility, and parliament should not divest itself of or evade its responsibility by handing it over to any set of individuals to deal with; otherwise the end will be requiescat in pace.
Let this house have the fullest investigation; let the report come back to parliament; and let the people's representatives from Vancouver to Halifax decide what should be done in the way of cooperation as suggested by the railway experts and others who are in a position to advise in this matter. I understand that Mr. Fairweather, of the Canadian National railway system, who is an expert and has the confidence of the Minister of Transport and of the officials associated with him, says that the greatest measure of cooperation has been put into effect since the act which was passed for that purpose was put on the statute book. If Mr. Fairweather's statement is correct, there cannot be a greater measure of cooperation than there is now or any greater speed than they are making to-day. To do more will only be forcing a willing horse to death and will go far to injure the future of this young country. When I say "young" I have in mind the Canadian west. I can well remember a speech of the late Hon. Robert Fofke, while leader of the progressive party, in which he referred to the east. That evening I reminded him of the fact that as a young man he came over as an immigrant to Canada, and that through his industry and his ability he became leader of the progressive party in this house and a member of the parliament of Canada, his country by adoption. But, I said, he should not forget the great men, from the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, including Sir Wilfrid

In making my choice between cooperation and unification I would support cooperation. I am sure that that is the feeling also of my constituents. I do not think the time will ever come when the people of Canada will be satisfied to hand our national railway over to a private monopoly.
In seeking the solution of our railway problem we must go further than merely to contemplate the abandonment of certain sections of existing lines, which would be done at the expense of the employees and the districts that these lines serve. In my constituency it is rumoured that the railway companies contemplate abandoning some lines adjacent to the city of Portage la Prairie. It is the general opinion that this is contemplated, but as yet the board of transport commissioners have not been notified of any action. The lines that it is proposed to abandon have in the last ten years transported some seven million bushels of grain, as well as considerable quantities of other farm produce such as hay and live stock. There are over a dozen loading platforms and three grain elevators along these lines. Their abandonment will mean something to the grain growers as well as to the employees, whose position should not be forgotten. Where they now have convenient loading platforms, and elevators within a short haul, if the lines are abandoned they will have to carry their grain by truck or wagon perhaps fifteen or twenty [Mr McKinnon.]
miles to Portage la Prairie, which will add considerably to the cost of producing and marketing the grain. It is something that we must keep in mind.
Reference was made to the interest charges being borne by our railways. I agree with other hon. members that we must make a more determined effort to scale down these interest charges and thus lighten the financial burden that the railways are now carrying. This should be done before we contemplate depriving employees of their livelihood or making it more difficult for districts to carry on their industry for lack of railway service. I think it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) who said something should be done about refunding the outstanding high interest bonds; with this I heartily agree. A newspaper printed in the maritime provinces-that country which produces so many wise men-the Fundy Fisherman, carried in its issue of December 14, 1938, an item headed, "Food for thought." It reads as follows:
There is a small issue of perpetual, i.e. eternity, bonds outstanding against the Canadian National Railways of about $70,000. The railway, i.e. the government, has already paid over $190,000 interest on these bonds, and still owes the original amount. This is a sample of the kind of financing with which our railways have to contend, and unless something is done about these bonds and similar issues, millions and millions of interest will continue to be paid without reducing the principal one nickel, in fact the interest is often reborrowed. Surely we do not need any further argument for refunding our railway debts than the above example.
I am quoting this to the house in order again to direct attention to the fact that we could save millions of dollars if we would make a real, honest-to-goodness attempt, to refund our outstanding railway bonds at the lower rates of interest now prevailing.

Even if we have to operate them at a loss, we must not lose sight of the fact that they are a public utility, a necessity, and must be maintained, unless our super-men, the presidents and directors of the railways, succeed in changing our climatic conditions, or do away with winters. In its editorial of April 27, the Ottawa Journal appropriately points out this aspect of the problem:
So with our railways. We hear a great deal (and we shall hear much more following Mr. Dunning's speech) about the "crushing burden" of the Canadian National. But do the people who talk stop to reflect upon what the Canadian National (and our railways as a whole) means to the country? What they mean in a country of such vast distances; what they mean in their contribution to national unity; what they mean in the facilitating of production that has placed Canada so high among the trading nations, and has given our people a standard of living which is amongst the highest in the world?
The truth is that the production of new wealth which has so benefited Canada would never have taken place if railways were not to be built unless they could pay operating costs and fixed charges, or were to be abandoned if they ceased to earn a profit. The truth, equally, is that if this country to-day started to tear up, or abandon or even degrade, all railway lines that do not earn an operating profit, it would be inviting the danger of retarding gravely the country's growth and development.
In other words, the dividends from our railways are in public value; the deficits what we pay for one of the most vital national services that the state can render its citizens.

The natural market for the farmers, merchants and manufacturers of the constituency of Lotbiniere is the city of Quebec. The municipalities having the greatest population and means of production are located on the shore of the St. Lawrence river, but unfortunately the only railroad at their disposal is the former Lotbiniere and Megantic. Do hon. members know in what way these municipalities are served? They are served by a small mixed train which leaves Parisville during the winter at seven o'clock in the morning. It does not go directly to Quebec via the Quebec bridge, but goes to Levis. This compels the farmers of Deschaillons and the neighbouring

Mr. Speaker, this is a good bill, founded as it is upon similar legislation in Great Britain which has been successful, within certain limitations, for a number of years. The purport of the bill is to facilitate cooperation between the two large railway companies in the reduction of track mileage, rolling stock equipment, elimination of terminals and so on. It will succeed in that way to the extent to which it reduces the opposition of the railway workers who would otherwise be thrown out of employment, and of such unions and other people as would sympathize with them. In that way it will facilitate the cooperation to which I have referred, but it must be obvious that to some extent it will have an opposite effect.
When a proposal for cooperation is made, each railway will naturally look at it from the point of view of the financial effect upon their body politic so to speak. If, in addition to the saving to be effected, or in contradiction to the saving, it is found that there will be a large outlay for pensions, it is possible that this might sway the balance and that there would be no cooperation in that particular instance. There is this to be considered, and I believe it has had some effect in England. Will the proposed legislation apply to companies which are not exactly subsidiaries of the main company but are under its control? I have in mind a railway on Vancouver island, the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway. Quite a number of years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway took it over, but they did not wish to acknowledge ownership and the railway was said to be leased. But as time went on, it became desirable from their point of view to admit a more definite control, and so they allowed that they held a predominant stock interest in the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway. subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 29, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
The mover of this bill, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), according to the explanatory note accompanying the bill, seeks to prohibit by statute the catching of salmon by the use of purse seines in the waters adjacent to the mouth of the Fraser river. In order to accomplish this purpose he is asking this house to pass a bill amending the Fisheries Act, 1932, which is the general act pertaining to fisheries. Section 1 of this bill reads as follows:
1. Section twelve of The Fisheries Act, 1932, chapter forty-two of the statutes of 1932, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:-
"(2) Seine fishing for salmon is prohibited within the boundaries of a line drawn from the extreme westerly point of Point Grey to the most northerly point of Galiano island; thence in a straight line to and following the international boundary line to the outer range light on said boundary; thence in a line drawn in a westerly and northerly direction to the point of commencement."
This, in other words, describes an area in the Gulf of Georgia immediately south of the mouth of the Fraser river, or to the point where the Fraser river empties into the strait, where for some years, that is from 1933, purse seining has been permitted under certain conditions at certain specific times in a limited way. The point in question is immediately to the north of the boundary or line dividing the United States waters from the Canadian waters in that area. The United States authorities have always permitted the use of seines to catch salmon there, and my information is that it is the method most employed by the fishermen of the United States to catch salmon in those waters. Naturally the Canadian fishermen, seeing the advantage of using purse seines in Canadian waters, sought for many years that privilege. But it was only in 1933, as a result of certain representations having been made to the then acting minister of Fisheries, that such method of fishing at that location was permitted by order in council.
In 1935 the hon. member for New Westminster sought by legislation, I believe, to prohibit absolutely this method of fishing in those waters. The bill which he then introduced was referred by the house to a committee, which, after looking into the matter
for some time, reported adversely. I understand the bill was defeated in the committee by a very narrow margin.
Then in 1936 the hon. member, with the persistence characteristic of his race, again brought before the house a bill seeking prohibition of purse seining in the same waters. After listening to his arguments, I asked the hon. member to give me time to look into the matter and devote more attention to the problem which he was bringing before the house, and which was new to me. He graciously agreed to my request and withdrew his bill on my undertaking that during the following season I would investigate the whole question, which I did in his company; and upon my return to Ottawa I saw to it that the area in which purse seining was permitted was reduced.
This, however, did not satisfy the hon. member, and during the session of 1937 he introduced legislation to bring about an absolute prohibition of purse seining in those waters. Again he withdrew his bill, and again the area was reduced, to its present size. At the present time the strip of water in which purse seining is permitted is only two miles wide, and I am told by those who are conversant with that method of fishing that this width is not sufficient to permit the successful operation of seine boats. For the benefit of hon. members who are not familiar with this .method of fishing, I may state that the gear for salmon purse seining on the Pacific coast, including the boat, the nets and all the apparatus, comprises quite an outfit. The boats are quite large, employing some twelve or fifteen hands-

la any event the time during which purse seining was permitted last year was very short. Nevertheless 105 boats came to those waters, much too large a number for the area. Since that time complaints have been made by fishing interests, or by people interested in fishing and purse seining, suggesting that the number of permits for purse seining in those waters should be restricted.
The contention now made is that these operations at the mouth of the Fraser river are detrimental to the fisheries and may tend to impair the ascent of fish up the river in sufficiently large numbers for reproduction purposes. But opinions on this matter, as on almost every other matter pertaining to fisheries, is divided. Some people contend that this method of fishing, under the limitations which have been imposed both as to area and as to time, is not injurious to the industry or to the fisheries generally. Some people contend that purse seining is the only method by which fish can be taken in that area because the water is too clear for successful gill net fishing, so they say there is no harm in permitting the purse seiners to take fish which otherwise would not be caught.

subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER
speechtext: Who offered that argument?

subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
Some people have advanced those views, and they are on record. Others contend that gill netting could foe carried on successfully in those waters and that purse seining crowds out quite a number of individual gill netters who otherwise would derive quite a revenue from these operations. Therefore they say the purse seining method of fishing is injurious to the gill netters.
The permits issued at the inception, in 1933, were justified on special grounds. At that time it was claimed that the late run of fish which frequented these waters in the fall, if not taken at the time, at the place and in the quantities possible only by means of purse seining, would not be of any value to the industry. Representations were made to the effect that if purse seiners were not permitted to take fish at that point it would be a loss to the industry, that if these fish were caught further up the river their physical state would be such that they would not make a first quality pack. On this point also there is a wide difference of opinion, and the true situation has never been ascertained definitely; or, in other words, it has not been possible to get the different factions to agree with regard to this point. We must not forget the fact that whether we prohibit or permit the use of purse seines in those waters, the fishermen of the United States who fish in the waters adjacent to the imaginary line Which forms the boundary will continue to operate seine boats and catch fish by that method.

On the other hand it is contended that were we to prohibit completely the use of purse seines in those waters, the gill netters or the individual fishermen farther up the river would have a chance to get at the fish, catch them and supply them to the packing industry in as good condition as it would be possible to get them in any other way.
The obvious object of the bill is by statute to prohibit one method of fishing, and to allow other methods to be used, subject to regulation by order in council. Many arguments are being advanced pro and con, and I suppose so long as purse seining is permitted, even in a limited way and over a limited area, those arguments will continue.
In 1938 the gill netters caught 1,526,117 sockeye, while the purse seiners caught 214,264.

speechtext:
Of the pinks, the fall variety or late run of fish, the gill netters caught 816, and the purse seiners, two. There is no doubt that the quantities of fish caught by the purse seiners in those areas have increased to a certain extent on account of the fact that a larger number of fishermen or fishing boats are resorting to those waters for the purpose of catching fish by that method. We are faced with this question: Will parliament sanction the principle of regulating or prohibiting by statute a method of fishing? Unless extraordinary circumstances are offered in favour of that course, I submit the practice hitherto followed by all governments and parliaments in Canada, acting under the Fisheries Act, is to continue regulation by order in council of the methods, the areas and the time of fishing.
I claim that the use of purse seines or any other gear for catching fish is a natural right which should be available to all who want to use or take advantage of that right, and that they should be permitted to choose whatever method they may wish to catch the fish. There is no particular reason offered why purse seines should be prohibited by statute. The use of purse seines is a natural method of catching fish resorted to by many people on the coast, and one which should be curtailed or limited only when the interests of the majority or of the public would require such action. But it seems in this instance that so far there is only a difference of opinion between two classes of fishermen as to who should have the first right to get at the fish.
There is, however, a further element in connection with the matter which has been advanced this year and which, I believe, should receive consideration. I believe the argument is not strong enough to support the adoption of the bill or to justify parliament in saying that this or any other method of

Fisheries Act-Seine Fishing
fishing should be prohibited by statute; but there is the argument advanced, supported by fact, that the area has been restricted within a very narrow compass. It is only two miles wide, and stretches across the strait from the mainland to the southern part of Valdes island. In that small area 105 boats fished last year, and I admit that was too large a number successfully to carry on. Also it involved too great an impact on the fisheries. We shall have either to restrict the area or enlarge it, or-and this is a further alternative-limit the number of boats which might resort to those waters to take advantage of that method of fishing in order to get at the late run of fish in the fall.
I feel, therefore, that at this time parliament would not be justified in adopting the extreme measure outlined in the bill; but now that the hon. member for New Westminster has brought to the attention of parliament a matter which he believes to be of vital interest not only to his constituents but to the public generally, and more particularly to the fishing industry of the Pacific coast, and specifically at the mouth of the Fraser river, he should be satisfied. I think, if the hon. member for New Westminster would withdraw this bill, ask the people in his constituency.to be content with the privileges they now enjoy and give the department a chance to look into this other aspect of the matter, that is the over-fishing of that area, he would have accomplished his purpose. A royal commission is to be appointed shortly to investigate certain aspects of our fisheries on the Pacific coast, and I would be disposed to refer this matter to that commission for consideration as soon as it is appointed. The commission could very well study the matter from every angle and it would have the evidence of those interested. A report could be made to the department as to whether purse seine fishing in those particular waters is likely materially to affect the run of pink and sockeye salmon in the Fraser river. If it is found that this is likely to occur, then it will be in the public interest to prohibit by regulation fishing by that method in those waters. I believe the hon. member should be satisfied to leave this matter to the department to be investigated during the summer from this new angle.

subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fishing on the Fraser river extends into my district and for a number of years there have been bitter complaints against the operation of purse seines at the mouth of the Fraser. It has been pointed out to me that as the salmon approach fresh water they form
into schools and remain there for some time, when along come the seine netters and scoop them up. This practice is claimed to be detrimental because it prevents fish from ascending the Fraser river in sufficient quantities to reach the spawning grounds. It is claimed to be most unfair to those men who are trying to make a living by fishing on the Fraser river. I think the minister has admitted that there may be too many boats or the district may be too small or too large.
The department has had an opportunity to go into this matter for a number of years, and I would have thought that after this government had been in power for four years something would have been done at least to satisfy themselves as to whether or not the case put before this house was correct. From my conversations with men engaged in the industry and with others who are interested, I am led to believe that purse seine fishing is detrimental to the salmon industry. I want to give my support to this bill at this time. The minister objects to this action being taken by statute, but that is the only method we have in the House of Commons to do anything of this kind when the government refuses to do it by regulation.

speechtext:
In the short time at my disposal I should like to place some certain information before hon. members. First of all, let me say that I appreciate the offer of 'the minister, although to be candid I must say that I am disappointed that he could not see fit to accept this bill. I am not presenting this case from a personal viewpoint, I am presenting it simply on behalf of an organized body of fishermen on the Fraser river. My persistence in bringing this up year after year is on account of the grave injustice that we feel is being done to the gill net fishermen on the Fraser river. Without any notification to the fishing industry or to members of parliament, this area was declared by order in council to be open for seine fishing, for the first time since confederation. It had always been a gill net fishing area; but the seine fishermen having depleted certain other areas, new areas had to be found and so the area of the mouth of the Fraser river was opened up to them. My reason for introducing a bill is to prevent anything being done other than by statute.
Fisheries Act-Seine Fishing

I want to prevent action similar to that taken in 1933 being taken in the future by order in council.
The minister referred to a royal commission which would investigate the dispute, but mentioned only the pink and sockeye salmon fishing. Unless the scope of its reference goes much further, I feel that the investigation will be all one-sided. I intend to show that this seine fishing has hurt not only the sockeye and pink varieties, but other varieties of fish as well, which were never intended to be taken in that area but are being taken. The answer made to our protests in 1933 was that quality fish was required and that the late run of sockeye and the variety of salmon known as pinks could be caught in better condition by the seines before they came into the river. I protested then, and protest now, and it has worked out exactly as I forecast. These seine boats take not only the late run of sockeye and pinks, but the main run of sockeye and other varieties of salmon as well. I have not the time to give all the figures before nine o'clock, and this is the last opportunity I shall probably have this session to air this grievance, but let me give a few figures to show the depletion which has occurred in the varieties of salmon extremely valuable to the gill net fishermen. The following figures show the catch on the
Fraser river:	1932	1937
	Cases	Cases
Red spring	. . . 19,994	3,622Pink salmon	... 3,622	84White spring	. . . . 11,020	1,738Blue back	. . . . 16,558	1,354Cohoe	. .. 28,685	11.242Chums	... 45,100	20.934
Those are the figures of the catch of other varieties of fish which mix with the great hordes of sockeye or pink salmon and are caught by the same seine fishermen.
The fishermen of the Fraser river are put to a great deal of expense for their nets and boats, and if they were allowed to fish for sockeye alone they could not exist at all. They have been catching other varieties and have done so for many years. But the drop in these varieties of spring salmon has been severe ever since the seine boats were allowed in the gulf of Georgia.
I am sure the minister will be interested in the figures shown in his latest report. They show that out of the total number of seining areas in British Columbia, twenty-seven in all, in areas 17, 18 and 19, in the strait and gulf of Georgia, 74,873 fish were taken by purse seines out of a total catch of 85,260 spring salmon caught by purse seines off the entire Pacific coast. I think there is a mistake 
in those figures, and that it should be pounds instead of number of fish. But if we take even the numbers of fish caught, it means that only 520 more spring salmon were caught in the remaining areas of British Columbia by all the seines that were operating. This shows conclusively that the greater proportion of spring salmon are caught right in the gulf of Georgia or in the waters of the Juan de Fuca strait after the fish pass the Sooke traps.
No protests whatsoever have been made by the industry this year, nor have any protests been made by the seine fishermen. It is true that there have been protests by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), but I do not think he was speaking officially on behalf of the seiners. He picked out some items from newspapers and quoted them when speaking to the bill. But, Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill I am speaking for the fishermen of the Fraser river. I do not think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was speaking on behalf of the industry. My information is that no representations were made directly to him to speak against my bill when he spoke on March 28 last. Let me deal for a moment with some of the arguments he used, and if one takes all the inaccuracies and untruths and what-not out of his speech on that occasion there is mighty little left.

Let me deal briefly with his speech on that occasion. He said that the waters down there are clear. His words were, "the water down there, I say without fear of contradiction is clear." Well, I can read a letter from the president of the British Columbia Fishermen's Protective Association absolutely denying that. He says he has fished down in those waters. But even if the waters were clear, which they are not, what did we witness when the trap question was up? The hon. member said that the gill net men could fish outside Sooke harbour. But in the committee he said, "No, those waters are muddy." What is the use of dealing with a man who jumps round like that? It is like a flea that jumps round all the time. It is difficult to pin the hon. member down to one position.
He said further that the waters there cannot be gill netted, that they never have been. Again I quote from a letter from the president who says:
I wonder what is wrong with old man Neill? He must have gone crazy when he says this area has never been gill netted. He did not make the same protests when they were taking the seines out of Barclay sound or Alberni canal.

Fisheries Act-Seine Fishing
To take the seines out of Barclay sound would have been all right with him. He could then say, "I can get them allowed in the gulf of Georgia for you, where there are more fish." Of course, there are more fish in the gulf of Georgia.

for that kind of an argument?

subtopic: SEINE FISHING FOB SALMON PROHIBITED IN THE WATERS ADJACENT TO MOUTH OF FRASER RIVER
speechtext:
I have a name for it, but the house would not allow me to use it; I hope to use it after the house is closed.
The statement that I have from the president of the fishermen's protective association is that the waters have always been fished by the gill net fishermen. Not only is it difficult for the gill net fishermen to fish there now, but many of them had their nets cut last year by the seines. The seine boats on their way back home ran amongst the gill nets, cutting the nets in two.
In 1922 a commission, of which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was a member, recommended something which is just as applicable to-day as it was then. The commission at page 19 of their report have this to say:
We think that an unlimited and widespread use of either purse or drag seines is a sure and quick way of depleting the supplies of salmon. But it was made clear to us that there are places on the coast outside of rivers where gill nets have not .as yet been proved to be effective in catching salmon in reasonable large quantities. With this in mind, therefore, we recommend that drag and purse seines be not permitted to be operated for salmon except where their use has been demonstrated to be the only effective and reasonably economic method of catching such fish.
Since confederation the gill net fishermen have been fishing in that area. The hon. member talks about clear waters. The waters are just about as clear as his argument, which is as clear as mud. I doubt if he has ever been there. I witnessed the fishing there last fall. Many of the nets of the seine boats were dragging on the bottom and bringing up everything in the shape of crabs and debris. The water is very shallow indeed and the seine boats should not be operated there. When they were allowed to go in there in 1933, some sixty-four went in. It was never expected or intended that nearly all the seine boats of British Columbia would swoop down on the area and take the fish.
We have heard a great deal about the traps both this year and last. I have supported the elimination of the traps because I believe they are detrimental to the fishing industry to the fishermen, but they are not nearly
as destructive as the seine boats in the gulf of Georgia because, while the trap has a lead which the fish follow, the seine boat is a mobile trap and can swoop down into the midst of a school of fish, throw a net around them and take up sometimes as many as ten thousand fish at one time. The seine is more dangerous and more destructive than any trap could be because the seine boat moves round following the school of fish wherever they may be. In 1933 some sixty-four seine boats went in there, and last year the total number was 105. If this is allowed to continue, not only will the great salmon fishery run of the Fraser river be depleted, but the gill net fishermen on the Fraser river will be deprived of the greater part of their livelihood.
I repeat, not only do the seines take sock-eye and pinks of every variety, but the seines in the gulf of Georgia take the greater proportion of the variety of salmon known as springs, a far greater proportion than is taken by seines from all other areas in British Columbia. In fact, nearly all the springs were taken from the area of the gulf of Georgia.
Bear in mind that only so many fish come in the strait of Juan de Fuca, and if you allow 105 seine boats to go among those fish when they are schooling and ready to head up the waters of the Fraser to spawn, it cannot but deprive, the gill net fishermen of part of their livelihood and damage the fishery. Allowing 105 seines will not bring in any more fish into the area; the numbers of fish are limited, and certain species have been decreasing. Therefore every seine boat you allow in there helps to deprive a gill net fisherman of part of his livelihood. Even if that were not the result, something would happen which is equally bad, namely, the destruction of many fish of different varieties which are heading up the headwaters of the Fraser to spawn. If the greatest good to the greatest number is the motive of any one person or any one party, he or they would not allow the seines to fish in the gulf of Georgia.
The minister- has proposed a commission. I suppose we shall have to accept it because it is better than refusing the bill itself. I feel sure the fishermen, when they are made aware of this will be satisfied to argue the case before the commission, provided the regulations drafted for the guidance of the commission are favourable and not too one-sided in favour of seining. I would again warn the minister not to confine the reference to pink salmon and sockeye only; let him include also
Fisheries Act-Seine Fishing

white springs, red springs, pink springs, cohoes and chums. Let him put these also in the order of reference and include the following:
Is it in the best interests of the salmon fishery of the Fraser river system that seine boats be allowed to operate in the gulf of Georgia?
Is it not a fact that the seines catch immature fish and likewise other varieties as well as sockeye and pinks?
Is it not a fact that the salmon congregate in the area in schools or large numbers preparatory to ascending the Fraser river to spawn; and is it not a -fact that the seines take advantage of this condition to catch the salmon in great numbers, at the same time breaking up these schools of salmon?
Has the continued operation of the seines in this area reduced the annual returns of the individual gill net fisherman, especially on white and red spring salmon, cohoes and chums?
Until 1933 was it not a fact that the waters of the gulf of Georgia were fished almost exclusively by individual gill net fishermen?
I also draw the minister's attention to this fact. Many men who were formerly in the fishing industry and had endeavoured to maintain themselves on small ranches along the banks of the Fraser river have been compelled-and I speak particularly of those above the bridge at New Westminster-to go back into fishing, and thus increases of fishing licences are noticed over the past few years. In 1930 there were 200 licences issued to those fishermen who had small ranches but who fished most of the time and also endeavoured to maintain a garden and some small stock on a small ranch. Later figures are: 1935, 229; 1936, 273; 1937, 318; and last year 407 of these licences were issued. I draw that to his attention 'because we maintain that, the more seines allowed in the gulf, the fewer fish will there be caught up on the waters of the Fraser by the gill net fishermen, and the fewer fish will there be for spawning.
Speaking for one moment as a member of the international pacific salmon fisheries commission, I can see a great difficulty when the time comes that we have to apportion fifty per cent of the Canadian catch. The Americans will be allowed fifty per cent on their side and they can apportion it as they see fit. But when we are called upon to distribute fifty per cent of the total catch on the Canadian side among the various types of gear, there is certainly going to be great difficulty in deciding how many of the fifty

per cent the seines will be allowed to catch and how many the gill netters will be allowed to catch.
This, Mr. Speaker, has always been a gill net area. In the past year many of the gill netters went further out than in former years, and with considerable success. Even if the waters were clear it would not deter the gill net fishermen from catching fish in that area, because they would fish mostly at night time, and there is no phosphorescence in the water there because the mud from the muddy waters of the Fraser precludes it in that particular part of the area.
We are not asking that seining be prohibited from the entire area of No. 17. There is still part of that area which, under the provisions of my bill, would be left out. That, of course, was overlooked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who said that if the bill passed there would be no seining in No. 1 district, it would all be confined to No. 2 and No. 3. "But I ask," he stated, "why should it be confined to two districts; why should it not be distributed over the three?" This, Mr. Speaker, relates to only part of the area, the part which the gill netters have used since the time of confederation, a part which can be easily gill netted by the individual gill net fisherman, but which has been prohibited to him by seines being allowed in on the gulf.
The first concession made in 1935 was a splendid one in its way. The second one, of course, took the seines out a little further. The present bill would take them clear out of the headwaters of the Fraser, clear entirely of that area where the fish assemble preparatory to ascending the headwaters of the Fraser to spawn; and remember it is in that little two-mile area that the seines make their great catch.
If I have persisted in my efforts on behalf of the gill net fishermen it is because, as pointed out in the opening remarks of my speech, we feel that seining in the area should never have been allowed. If the matter of the opening up of the area had come before the fisheries committee, or before the house, I feel sure that the area would never have been opened at all. It is true that in 1935, when the matter was discussed before the fisheries committee, we lost, but only by one vote. The chairman of that committee, who is not now a member of the house, told me that had the vote been a tie he for one would have given the deciding vote in favour of the gill net fishermen and eliminating the seines.

When we were dealing with this item last night, I asked the minister if he could give any explanation why no attempt had been made to give effect to the recommendations of the committee on industrial and international relations which looked into this matter in 1936.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
My hon. friend refers, I think, to the request that has been made repeatedly, perhaps more by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), with regard to employing Canadian seamen instead of orientals. The explanation has been given quite frequently. One of the reasons is, of course, that on these vessels travelling to the orient there are a great many oriental passengers, and it is thought that white men do not care to serve orientals. Another reason given by the steamship company is that it would be extremely expensive to rearrange their accommodation on the ships, they would have to make provision for the two classes of people; and whether it may be regarded as a good reason or not, it would mean also a very large increase in the expenditure for labour; in fact, so much so that I think practically the whole amount they are now obtaining as subsidy would disappear. This is a question that has been debated from year to year. As I stated last night, the company has agreed to take on a number of boy seamen, and, I think, have employed some twenty-four. After the report of the committee came in, an investigation also was made, in which I think it was pretty clearly shown that it would be quite impossible to obtain a sufficient number of qualified
men to serve on these ships. I know that statement has been contradicted, but our own officials made some investigations and I think the claim of the company in that respect is pretty well founded.
Not as to boys; there are plenty of boys.

No, I am not referring to boys; the company are putting on boys. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company state that their experience has shown that from the point of view of both adequate supply of labour and the competitive conditions with which they are faced in this service-they are competing with subsidized boats from Japan and the United States-it is neither practicable nor economically possible to adopt the policy asked for by my hon. friends. They made a further reply from which I give these extracts:
I can assure you that if it were practicable al)9 economically possible it would be the policy ot the company to comply with the request. However our experience has shown that from the standpoint both of an adequate supply of labour and of the competitive conditions with which the company is faced in this service it is neither practicable nor economically possible to adopt such a policy at present.
According to the report of the departmental representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce following the investigation made, there were only forty-five competent and suitable deckmen available in Vancouver and seventeen in Victoria, or a total of sixty-two.
The shipping master at Vancouver reported only yesterday-
This is 1937.
-that the situation regarding unemployed seamen is unchanged and that lie has practically no inquiries from seamen seeking employment. Ihe manager of the sailors' home states that there are fewer unemployed whom he describes as unemployable, and some boys who have had a few voyages on seasonal employment on coastal vessels, and some of them are finding employment in camps.
The whole gist of the matter is that from the point of view both of expense and of a sufficient supply of seamen the company does not feel that it can comply with the request. I would be glad myself if it were possible to employ all white men. At the same time I think most of these Chinamen who are employed on these boats are British subjects, coming mostly from Hongkong.
This question has come up from year to year. I do not know that I can add anything further. I think that by and large the attitude taken by the company is fairly reasonable.
Supply-Trade-Subsidies

I am not greatly concerned about the colour of the men engaged on these ships. What I am concerned about is that the orientals are engaged because they can be hired cheaply, that this company is manning its ships with orientals to take advantage of cheap oriental labour, while getting a substantial subsidy from the Canadian government. Further, I am not greatly impressed with the statement that there are no unemployed trained seamen at the port of Vancouver. How are we going to get trained Canadian seamen, or trained white seamen, if we engage on our ships oriental seamen exclusively? It takes experience as a seaman, actual time working on board ship at the various kinds of work on a ship, to become experienced. Until we give men an opportunity to become experienced, we shall not have experienced men, either with or without employment.
I wish to refer to the 1936 report of the committee on industrial and international relations. The reference to the committee was a resolution moved by the hon. member for New Westminster, namely, the question of the employment of Canadian citizens on ships and vessels the owners or charterers of which receive moneys from the public treasury of Canada. The committee heard evidence and made recommendations not only in regard to ships on the Pacific coast but also in regard to ships on the Atlantic coast. I do not know whether the parts of the report that referred to the Atlantic coast have been implemented, but I do know that the part which referred to the Pacific coast has not been implemented. I should like to read briefly from this report, found at page 461 of the votes and proceedings for 1936. There were three statements made, and the third one reads as follows:
Oriental shipping: the third type is chiefly carried on by the Empress boats of the Canadian Pacific Railway transpacific service. These ships receive a substantial subsidy from the government. The total number of men employed to man them is 2,033, of whom 265 are white British, engaged as officers and engineers. The remaining 1,768 are Chinese, comprising 277 deckhands, 558 in the engine room, and 933 victuallers. It is claimed by the company that, as much of their passenger trade, namely, 67 per cent, through and local, is oriental, this type of labour is not only cheaper but infinitely more satisfactory than -white labour, since the latter could not be gotten to cater to oriental passengers on the one hand, or mix with oriental labour on the other. It is moreover claimed by the company that the service is now supplied at a serious yearly loss, and that the extra cost involved in the substitution of Canadians for orientals would make the service practically impossible of operation.
Your committee therefore recommend-

Here we have the recommendations of the committee, which I submit were reasonable:
1.	That, in view of the substantial subsidy granted yearly to the Canadian-Australian line by Canada, the small number of Canadians employed in its service be brought to the attention of the company, and that they be requested to afford Canadian seamen a reasonable degree of employment at the earliest possible convenience.
I did not read the submission in regard to the Canadian-Australian line:
2.	That, as up to the year 1913 the decks of the Empress boats were manned by white seamen, and inasmuch the deck service is an important and responsible branch of the work of these boats, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company be requested to replace the orientals now- so employed by Canadian seamen, and that this change be made at the company's earliest opportunity.
The committee realized that the company had some difficulties to contend with and consequently did not ask that the company should change at once from orientals to white seamen. We did suggest, however, that the deck hands, who at that time comprised only 227 of the 2,033 men required to man these ships, should be Canadian citizens of the white race. I do not think that was unreasonable, and I believe we should insist that the company do something to fulfil these very reasonable recommendations before any further subsidy is granted.

Not only was the recommendation just read by the hon. member adopted by this house; the following year, when I introduced the same resolution, the minister was in Australia on behalf of the government and the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that if the bill were withdrawn he would set up a committee on the Pacific coast to ascertain if the statement made by the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway were true; that is, that there were not enough men to fill the vacancies in the deck service if the Chinese were displaced. That committee went out to the Pacific coast and held various meetings. I do not know where the minister got the report he read a few moments ago. If I had time I could get from my office the report of the committee I just mentioned, which recommended that there were sufficient experienced seamen to man the decks of two of these vessels. They also recommended-this was in 1937- that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company be asked to carry out the recommendations which were adopted by this house, and which were just read by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East that pressure should be brought to bear

Supply-Trade-Subsidies
upon this company, because I claim they have defied a report of this house. It may not have been an order, but it came as close as possible to being one. There are able-bodied seamen walking the streets of Vancouver who would be only too glad of an opportunity to work on one of these ships. The statement made by the minister that the Chinese sailors are British subjects from Hongkong has been exploded so often that I hardly need to do it again. No one who knows the situation in Hongkong would seriously put forward the argument that a Chinese from there was a British subject. There is a certain section of that city known as the white section, while the outlying parts are Chinese, and there is just a barbed wire separating the two. A Chinaman goes under the wire into the white section and is signed on by the number one man of the Canadian Pacific ship. Then the company claims that he, having come from Hongkong, is a British subject. The whole thing is ridiculous. Proof of that is seen in the fact that when these ships arrive in Vancouver, there are police on hand to see that none of these seamen leaves because the Canadian Pacific are responsible-I believe they are under bond of $500 a head-for none of these seamen escaping. None could prove his British citizenship or even his birth within the white settlement of Hongkong. So I appeal to the minister to study this matter seriously, because I am sure there are on the Pacific coast enough men to man the decks at least. We should not be voting $600,000 for this company and at the same time allow them to employ 2,033 men from China on these ships while our own people are walking the streets.

I do not know that I can add a great deal to what I have already said.
I have before me some comments by the company, and a note that the Department of Trade and Commerce asked the Department of Labour to verify some of the statements that were made. I might, in any event, read this short quotation:
The shipping master stated that he had few inquiries from seamen for employment on deep-sea vessels because there were no appointments available. The only deep-sea sailors being engaged in Vancouver are men to replace those who may occasionally be left behind by British and foreign vessels calling at British Columbia ports.
I might again mention the difficulties to which I referred previously. This line is in competition with a Japanese line which engages only Japanese sailors, of course at very low wages, and which receives a subsidy of something over S800,000. It is also in competition -with United States vessels, which are
very, very heavily subsidized. If the white men really can be obtained, the only alternative would be to increase the subsidy very heavily; otherwise probably the ships would fail to operate. There is an investment in these ships amounting to some $20,000,000, and in recent years the profit has been extremely small, while in many years there was no profit at all. That argument may not appeal to some people who think perhaps wages should come ahead of dividends, if you want to put it in that way, or interest on capital; but, after all the people who have the capital are not compelled to use it in that way. Certainly it would not be in the interests of this country to have a Canadian line driven off the Pacific in favour of a Japanese or United States line. I recall that two or three years ago one line which operated between New Zealand, Australia and San Francisco had to go out of business, and for some time there has been a real danger that the Canadian-Australasian line, in connection with which it was proposed a year or two ago to build two new ships, also would have to discontinue service unless something was done. In order to construct new vessels they required support from this government. As I said last night, that proposal has been abandoned for the time being because the cost of building vessels at the present time is too great.
It practically comes down to this:	The
company claimed they could not obtain enough seamen to man all the Empress boats, of which there are four. It might be possible- this has reference to the conditions which prevailed a year or two ago-to obtain sufficient men to man the decks of one of the boats, but the company claims that you cannot mix orientals and white men. You cannot put them in the same quarters; you cannot feed them at the same tables, and it would be impracticable to have white men on one boat and orientals on all the others. Again there is the matter of expense, which may or may not appeal to members of the house. Certainly I think it would be creating a considerable difficulty for the company, and frankly I have not felt disposed to insist upon that. They possibly would not accept the subsidy and might even discontinue the service.
But I am always of opinion that we ought to be reasonable in these matters. It is entirely necessary that we have the best of service and seamen on these vessels-and I am not going to cast any reflection upon the white people. But when we read of what takes place on some of the boats of other

Supply-Trade-Subsidies
countries, I think we must agree that the Canadian Pacific boats are manned and conducted in a way entirely superior to those of other countries-and I must add that I have no particular brief for the Canadian Pacific boats.
I, for one, do not care to take any chance of interfering with the efficiency of those boats, and I think the committee might very well pass the estimate. If in another year the committee feels disposed to suggest that this vote of $600,000 be doubled, well and good; but I would not recommend that to the government or to the House of Commons. On previous occasions I have spoken personally to the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and have impressed upon him the desire of parliament that more white men should be employed; and I think it is quite true to say that the Canadian Pacific would like to do so. But, as they say, they find it is impracticable. I am quite willing to continue pressing, in the hope that we may have more success than we have had in the past.
I must say I am not greatly impressed with the arguments the minister has used.
I would not expect the hon. member to be.

But I am sure he tried to make a good argument. He has said that some people may think that wages should come before dividends; that after all., the companies did not necessarily have to invest their capital in this way. Well, I think the minister is intelligent enough _ to know tlmt in these days people are finding great difficulty in investing their capital. They cannot be "choosy," and they will be less "choosy" in the future than they &ie to-day.
They do not invest unless they can get a return.

That is correct; but
when that capital is a means by which the people of the country must live, and when that capital is, itself, socially produced or socially created, the government of the people will have to see that that capital is used, whether the company likes it or not-because the living of the people will depend upon it, and demand it.
If we take the position that just because of the additional cost this company are not going to be compelled to employ on their ships help to whom they will have to pay a decent wage, wages that will enable them to take part in the life of their community as citizens, having a decent standard of living,

then the same argument can be applied to every other industry, and we could bring in millions of Chinese under guard to operate our factories. There was a time about ten or fifteen years ago when orientals were working in bond on the ships of the British Empire Steel Corporation. The same could be done with any industry in Canada, if we wish to do it in that way.
But is that the way in which the government or the people of this country want to see their industries operated? After all, the Canadian Pacific Railway is only another industry. It is a great industry, and one which receives substantial revenue from the Dominion of Canada. It is an industry that is made possible because the people of this country use the service it offers. So I say some effort should be made to improve the condition of the men employed, and if the Canadian Pacific Railway will not engage white seamen, at least they should be compelled to pay decent wages to the men they employ. The moment we compel them to do that, they would engage white seamen.

Would my hon. friend tell me how he would "compel" this company to pay wages of any kind? All one can do is withdraw the subsidy. And I should like to say, if the hon. member will permit me, that I am not going to be placed in a position where I am represented as being opposed to fair wages being paid to any man, whether he be a white man or one of any other colour. That is not the attitude I take.
My hon. friend speaks about "compelling" capital. Well, I am afraid that at that point there comes a radical difference between us. That perhaps can be done under the system of socialism which he advocates. But I would point out to him that we are not yet operating under that system. I am not a socialist-although I must confess that sometimes I am accused of entertaining some rather radical ideas, and that in some respects I do agree with the hon. member. But I must repeat that we are not yet in a position where we can compel capital to do so and so-and certainly not with this company, because it is not located within Canada.
May I make this further point:	A large
proportion of the passengers on these boats are orientals, and possibly they would have a right to say that they would like to 'be served by people of their own race.
There is nothing more I can do in the matter. The committee is faced with this proposition: If we are not prepared to give a subsidy unless the men are changed and unless only white men are employed on these

Supply-Trade-Motion Pictures
vessels, we could withhold the subsidy. But I do not think we would be justified in doing that, under the circumstances. I am perfectly willing again-and repeatedly-to make such representations as I can to induce the company to use as many white Canadian seamen as possible. Failing that, then it is just a matter of deciding whether or not we are going to wipe out the subsidy of $600,000. For my part, and so far as the government is concerned, I would say that we are not prepared to do that.

When I used the word "compel" I had in mind that we could give a subsidy conditionally. If they do not think the subsidy worth while they could refuse it. I have not looked up the report, but if my memory serves me correctly there is an enormous difference between the wages paid to white seamen by the Canadian Pacific and those paid orientals.
True.
And, again if my memory serves me correctly, they would be able to employ nine orientals for the wages they would pay one white seaman. United States ships are operating
With large subsidies.
-with white seamen.
And with large subsidies.
Let me tell the minister that the wages for officers and men on United States ships, in both the local and deep-sea service, are very much higher than the wages paid on Canadian vessels.
And so are the subsidies.
Yes, but if they would-
And the service is not as good.
Well, of course that is a matter of opinion.
But it is the truth.
It is not a matter of opinion; it is a matter of knowledge to anyone who has travelled on the coastal steamers of the Canadian Pacific. I have been going up that coast for forty years; I know.

Well, I have not travelled on the Canadian Pacific boats, so I cannot say just what the service is like. But I have travelled on the United States coastal boats from Vancouver to California, and the service on those boats is good enough for me and, I think, good enough for anybody. But if a person would rather have a number of obsequious,
cringing, servile individuals waiting on him, rather than a person who stands up like a man-well, if that is what he wants, he is entitled to that kind of service. For myself, I do not want it. I prefer service of a different kind. Those who want the other kind of service can have it, if they like-and they will get it cheaply, and plenty of it. Our ancestors were not of a servile race, and we hope that our children will always keep their heads up as men. I hope that before the government brings down these estimates again that something be done to get the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to show some respect for the recommendations of this House of Commons.

As the committee may know, it was decided that no further additions should be made to the building on Sussex street, and it became necessary to provide new laboratories at a different location. Approximately $1,500,000 is to be expended under this item. The minister tells us that these laboratories are to be constructed on a new location of 100 acres approximately two miles from the centre of the city.
It may not be that far.

There probably are good
reasons why these buildings should be located so far from the parliament and other government buildings, and I should like to know what they are. As other hon. members have

Supply-Trade-National Research
stated on previous occasions, some effort should be made to centralize the government buildings. I do not approve spreading out these buildings so far because they have to be visited by many people.

While there will be an administration building, these are mainly research buildings. It is desirable where they are carrying on research work of various kinds that they have a quiet place, and with pure air, it is suggested to me. They need a large area, and if it were to be obtained very close to the city it would be tremendously expensive.
Does it need 100 acres?
The 'board seems to think so.
Which board?
The national research council.

When new public buildings are erected, is there not some coordination between the various departments to ensure proper planning for the construction of government buildings, whether in the centre of the city or elsewhere? I do not like the idea of one department putting a building up here, and another department putting another up there. I was under the impression that now we had an experienced planner in the city, a proper planning scheme for government building construction would be worked out.

It is not a building at all of the same kind as departmental buildings. It is for mechanical and experimental work of various kinds. They have to have wind tunnels, for instance. While I do not know much about the technical requirements, my hon. friend can readily understand that testing engines, wind resistance, and all that sort of thing, and the building of tunnels for the purpose, require a considerable area, and they go further out in order to obtain sufficient space for their purposes.
Do they do these things outside the building or .within the building?

I do not suppose the tunnels are in the building. All sorts of experimental work is being carried on. My hon. friend has me at a bit of a disadvantage because I air. not familiar with scientific work, but I do know that the national research council, besides conducting many experiments, is doing a great deal of work for the industries of Canada for which they receive considerable revenue. Last year they collected something like 1103,000 for work they did for industrial concerns, making experiments with regard to met-als, machinery and that kind of thing. They also do a great deal of experimental
work in connection with wheat and grains generally, work that is beneficial to agriculture; also work for the various departments of government, more particularly the Department of National Defence, which has expanded tremendously, and if the work it requires to be done had to be done by industrial concerns it would mean a tremendous expense to that department. A great deal of that work is being done by the national research council. They also have a health branch and make investigations with regard to health, grain, forests, and fifteen or twenty other activities of a scientific kind. The men in charge of the national research council are qualified men drawn from all over Canada, and they are in charge of this work.
But unless you control them they will expand so rapidly and to such a size that research will become a nightmare to take care of.

Has the minister given
personal attention to the cost of this building? I wish to emphasize the necessity of the minister giving personal attention to expenditures on public buildings. Throughout the country-I do not say this in any political way at all-there is a strong feeling that a great deal of money is being spent on buildings in the city of Ottawa, and that this expenditure might be cut down to some extent. Here is a building costing about SI,500,000. Then we have the supreme court building, costing nearly S3,500,000. Actually the cost of the supreme court building is as much as the assessed value of one of the townships in my riding. That gives one some idea of the expenditure which is being made here on public buildings. I would be the last to criticize expenditure that was made in the right direction, and I am not in a position to criticize this particular building, but I do point out that where large expenditures of this kind are being incurred, the minister, with his knowledge of business, should apply some of that knowledge to make sure the money is well spent and that not too much of the taxpayers' money goes into it.

The board in charge of all
this work is composed not only of scientists but of some prominent businessmen in this country.

To whom are they
responsible ?

They are responsible to a
committee of the cabinet of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is chairman, so that whatever they recommend must first

Then there is Mr. W. R. Campbell, president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. My hon. friend will agree that he is a well qualified man.

The board selected the site, certainly.

I will see.
