spread over two years.

I should like to say a
word or two with reference to these public buildings, having in mind particularly the supreme court building, which will be under discussion when the appropriate estimate is before us. Did the department select an outside architect to draw the specifications for the proposed research building, or was it done by the public works architect?

I am not sure who drew
the plans but the Department of Public Works is undertaking the construction of the building.

Did the Department of
Trade and Commerce specify any of the mechanical equipment that is to enter into the construction of the building?

They intimate what the
building is to be provided for, and plans are drawn to meet the requirements.

If I were in the minister's place and had anything to do with the construction of that building I would see that it was constructed properly. With reference to the supreme court building, it is interesting to my mind what has taken place there. I imagine that if the building had been designed by our own architects the general plan that is being followed in the construction of government buildings would have been followed, but that is not the case with the supreme court building.
This national research building is to be erected outside Ottawa, and its construction will require a great deal of supervision. It is up to the head of the department to see that the building is properly constructed, and
[Mr. Euler.1
that the plans and specifications are wide open. I do not think any government building should have the plans and specifications tied up so that only one manufacturer can supply the mechanical material. I say to the minister that he should write a letter to the Department of Public Works directing that departs ment to see to it that the specifications be kept wide open in reference to all the mechanical equipment entering into the construction of that building, so that any one of half a dozen firms can figure on the material, instead of having only one firm supply mechanical equipment as is the case with the supreme court building.

I do not know why my hon. friend should assume for one moment that anything of that kind is contemplated. With regard to the minister of this department exercising supervision over the construction of the building itself, the actual construction, as my hon. friend knows, is the duty of the Department of Public Works.
This department has no control over the cost of the building at all?

This department is not particularly concerned with the construction once the plans are approved. Would my hon. friend expect that the minister could be particularly helpful in laying out and planning for a building which has to do with services such as these:	aeronautical research, asbestos
research, building and construction industry, electrical committee, field crop diseases, fire hazard testing, forestry research, grain research, hydraulic research, magnesian research, magnetite research, mining research, national building code, national committee on fish culture, parasitology, plant hormones, radio research, rubber and metal research, storage and transport of food, wood research, compressed gas cylinder research, corrosion research, and so on. I am quite free to admit that I know very little about these things. Certainly I would not be able to design any building to take care of these services.
And the minister has not any knowledge that they require this space at all.
Why, certainly.
I would not expect him to. I am not condemning him.

Under the law constituting the national research council the work of supervision and conducting the council is placed under the control of a board of men whose names I can give here. These men are supposed to be qualified to do the work

Supply-Trade-National Research
for which they were appointed. They have as their head Major General McNaughton, in whom I have a great deal of confidence. He was appointed by the former government. I believe he is a very competent man. And if we have confidence in these men-
But they all have extravagant ideas. That is the difficulty with men of that type.
I am afraid that my hon. friend is not exactly speaking from experience, or at least he is taking for granted something which perhaps he is not quite justified in taking for granted.

The minister, in answering one or two questions I put to him, made it appear that I was not altogether in favour of this extension of the work of the national research council. I am very much in favour of extending the work of the national research council, because I believe they are doing excellent work. I have some knowledge of what they have done in research and other lines, and I should like to see their activities extended because I believe they are a great benefit to the dominion.
In this connection, however, there is one point I should like to make. It is directed not particularly to the minister 'but to the government as a whole. In choosing and laying out sites of buildings we should make some effort to coordinate all the government structures in and around Ottawa. For instance, it seems to me that the selection of a site which they purchased some time ago, in the direction of Rockcliffe, was not good policy; I refer to the places where the bureau of statistics and the national research council are located. A few years later, when the government decided upon another building as a sort of adjunct of the research council building on Sussex street, they put it two miles away. I do not know anything about these matters. I realize that we in this chamber have to rely largely on the information we receive from the minister, and he in turn has to rely on the information he receives from the officials. But I do not know as yet whether the national research council recommended the site and whether they also recommended the purchase of 100 acres. We are told that they require tunnels and so on. I do not know whether they require those tunnels to be built on a large new area; they have, I believe, tunnels in some form at the present time in the research council building. It seems to me that if possible these buildings should be concentrated in an area where they would be easily accessible to all concerned.
I do not know that, beyond what the minister sajts, there is any special reason why this building should be two miles away from the centre of the city.
It is, for one thing, a matter of fire hazard where experiments are being carried on.

There is not the same danger of fire. We are taking it away from there.

Yes.

The large building remains there for other purposes.

When we are planning for the erection of government buildings, let that planning be done in some coordinated way so that it will be convenient for the people who have to use the building and good policy, I think, for the city of Ottawa. That does not apply merely to the Department of Trade and Commerce, because I believe the minister administers that department, as he has administered any department of which he has had control, in an efficient way.

I should like to direct a question to the minister with reference to the break-down of this expenditure for 100" acres of land. What amount of money is being paid; is the area 100 acres or 150 acres; and of what does it consist?

Government of the Yukon Territory-
133.	Administration, $45,000.

Naturally I must say to the minister that I specially regret the decrease that the department has seen fit to make in the Yukon allowance. The Yukon is charged up with so many expenses-telegraph lines in northern British Columbia, while other expenses are lumped together with the northwest-so that I sometimes wonder exactly what is Yukon, what is the northwest and what is northern British Columbia.
From 1898 to 1937 and 1938 about $225000,000 in gold was brought out from the Yukon. Silver production from 1925 approximated $14,000,000. There was no previous record. Lead up to date amounts to over $3,000,000.
Customs duties collected from 1898 amount to over $8,000,000. In 1938, 60,000 pelts were shipped out from the Yukon, consisting of marten, mink, lynx, ermine, fox and muskrat, and good taxes were paid on all those.
To date the government have expended a little less than $35,000,000 on the Yukon, so it seems to me that the amount which has been produced by the Yukon is a fairly good return on that expenditure by the government. Of course the minister may say the return is indirect, but at the same time when one considers the number of people who have

Supply-Mines and Resources
come out from the Yukon and bought farms in British Columbia and the middle west with money made in that territory, I think we are doing fairly well for Canada at large.
It was with great regret that I learned recently of the destruction of the Indian school at Carcross. That school has done good work. It was too small for the work it was expected to do. The building was owned by the government, and I am told that it will be impossible for the government to replace that school this year, because they have- perhaps not expended all their money, but decided where the money they have to spend will go. I would ask the minister to consider carefully this question of rebuilding that Indian school. It has done a good work. They have brought in those boys and girls, they have splendid instructors, and at that school in particular I know they teach the Indians so that when they go back to their ordinary surroundings they know how to go on with the work that men and women living in a natural state should know.
I would particularly ask the minister, when he sends his geological survey parties into the Yukon this year, to see that they keep an eye on the lode deposits in the Carmacks district. There are about twenty or twenty-five men working there now. It is the first satisfactory result from gold quartz mining in the Yukon. They have been working against great odds this year because of lack of water, on account of a light snowfall. They are twenty miles over a bad trail from the Yukon river, bad enough in winter and impossible in the summer. At the second run of the mill put in there by a few men, eighty-eight ounces of gold were processed, and twelve tons of concentrates, although for four months they were able to run only four to six hours daily. This district particularly needs a road in from the river, and if the geological survey party visits there doubtless the minister will be thoroughly informed that good work is being done. In the winter the transportation is not very difficult because it can be done by tractor, but when the thaw comes it is impossible.
It is only recently that people living there have put in the radiophone. A severe accident happened there this winter. A young man was badly burned, they had to walk twenty miles to the river before they could get in touch with the telegraph to call for a plane from White Horse, and after several days the man was brought down and taken by plane to White Horse.
Last year they had in the Yukon over five thousand tourists, with practically no
advertising save by the transportation companies, the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific and the White Pass. Tourists mean a great deal to us in the Yukon. The big-game hunters go there in larger numbers each year. Our guides are complaining of the destruction of game by wolves and coyotes. Two packers lost forty horses last winter by depredations of wolves. At one time we had a bounty on wolves and coyotes.
The money that is sent to us by the government is used for roads, hospitals and our out-of-works. Our young people are not out of work; but people who went into that country in 1898, as I did, are growing older, their health is failing, they must be taken care of. I can say no words of too great praise for work the sisters of St. Ann are doing at St. Mary's hospital. They look after tlm aged and unfit just as gently and as lovingly as if those men and women had any amount of money. They are indigent patients, people who are too old, too ill or too unfit to work, and they must be looked after. A number of years ago, when Lord Byng went into the territory, he said to my husband, "Captain Black, you represent the only truly socialistic constituency in the British empire." My husband looked at him and replied, "Your excellency, we are not socialists up here." To this Lord^Byng said, "Oh, yes; you are socialists in the truest sense of the word. You have practically no class distinction. You have no very rich and no very poor. You all work as long as you can and then, when you are unable to work, you take care of each other."
That is still true in that great country. We are so isolated that I sometimes think the government hardly understand our needs and conditions. The aeroplane and radio have annihilated time and space, and for that we should be thankful. The minister is a western man, who knows what hardship is, who has had to fight nature. Perhaps if he would take enough time to visit us in the north-I do not think it would take more than a week-he would understand our conditions better than they have been understood by any other minister. He has lived in the great open spaces, and I should like him to come to the north country as well as the parties he sends.
I am sure he would be welcomed, not only by me as a " half-baked opposition member," as I have been called, but also by his friends and my friends. We would see that he learned the country at first-hand.
I particularly ask the minister to be as generous as he can with us. We need help; we need money. Living conditions are difficult and expenses are very high. People who

Supply-Mines and Resources
bring up children in that country must send them out if they want them to have a college education. We have so many expenses in the north that people here do not have. A year ago my son and his wife visited me; my daughter-in-law had done the housekeeping while they were here, and she said to me one day, " Mother Black, you have good turkeys here." I replied that they -were very nice turkeys. She said, " I think Donald and I would like a turkey for dinner," so I said, "Lovely; just order it." Later she came to me and said, "Did you know how much the turkey would cost?" I said, "Yes; I suppose about 95 cents or a dollar a pound." She said, "Yes, the turkey cost $12.75, and I really feel as though I had eaten money." So when the minister pinches a little with us I wish he would remember our turkey. I wish he would remember how much we have to pay for what we buy. Lettuce comes in iby aeroplane now and the transportation costs thirty-six cents a head. We in the Yukon like fresh vegetables just as much as people like them here. We need help for our roads, for our mines, for our hopsitals, for our schools; we need help to do away with the predatory animals, the wolves and coyotes that are a menace and a danger to the camps. With the amount the minister has, I am sure he will exceedingly regret having pinched us^jown this year. He did very well for us last year, but now, like all hon. members, I come with hands outstretched, saying, " Gimme, gimme, gimme "1

The Yukon always has an earnest advocate in the person of the hon. member who now represents it. I hasten to assure her that the picture is not really quite so gloomy as she surmises from these estimates. It is true that under this item there is a reduction of $3,000, which is on account of the fact that it is anticipated that fewer mental cases will require treatment. Such eases must be taken to Vancouver, and of course we are always anxious to cut down expenditures wherever we reasonably can.
The other point mentioned by the hon. member in that regard really has to do with the next item, in which there is a reduction of $20,000, but I might say a word about that now. This does not represent the entire expenditure in the Yukon. My officers advise me that we have appropriated $40,000 under another vote for the construction of roads, which I think will bring the total amount nearer to that voted last year.
With regard to the Indian school, which unfortunately burned down a few weeks ago, our estimates for the year had been prepared when that occurred. I understand that fairly satisfactory arrangements have been made to

carry on the work, and I can assure my hon. friend that this matter will receive consideration next year, if I still have responsibility for this department. I mention that simply to give an encouraging thought to my hon. friends who sit opposite, although I fear very much that their hopes will not be realized.
In regard to the gold deposits in the Carmacks district I may say that Doctor Bostock, the geologist who has been in charge of the parties we have sent there for several years, has prepared a special report on the mineral production and outlook in the Yukon, which will be published shortly. I may tell my hon. friend that her remarks to-night will be particularly drawn to the attention of the deputy minister and of Doctor Bostock, who is now on his way into the Yukon for this season's work, and we shall be happy to cooperate as far as possible in meeting the suggestions she has made.
The hon. member referred to the difficulty of keeping down the predatory animals, the wolves and coyotes, in the Yukon district. The Yukon council, which is the local governing body, derives all the revenue that comes from the royalties on fur, and that being the case, we thought they should be able to make some provision for bounties to assist in the destruction of these wolves. However, that suggestion will receive consideration also. The Jion. member was kind enough to invite me to pay a visit to the Yukon. It is a pretty long distance away, and it is a large country to cover. I shall be happy to take this suggestion under consideration also, and if I could persuade my colleague the Minister of Justice to come with me I would be happy, if at all possible, to accept the invitation.
I particularly wish to express my thanks to the department and to the minister because they have always been so very kind to me and have always at least taken my suggestions under advisement.

1ST. Forest products laboratories, $151,109.

When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) was presenting his estimates a few minutes ago, he referred to the fact that in the new laboratoiy to be erected by his department they wdl be experimenting with forest products. Are we to have two departments looking after the same matter, each one spending a large sum of money to do the same work?

No. The national research council have nothing to do with the administration of this vote, beyond at times acting

Supply-Mines and Resources
in a consulting or advisory capacity. I recall that a year ago there was some discussion on this vote when the then leader of the opposition suggested that it should be merged with the work of the national research council. It has been conducted wholly apart from the work of the council.
I would say briefly that there is one laboratory at Montreal which deals especially with scientific investigations in connection with the manufacture of pulp and paper, and gives assistance to our important paper industry. Then, there is one on the Pacific coast which studies and examines the woods of British Columbia which are of a different type from those in eastern Canada. The third laboratory is in Ottawa. The studies made in these various laboratories have to do with the most efficient utilization of wood products and economies that can be developed, and deal with the handling and use of those products, and general scientific work of that kind.
While I admit that there is room for argument on the point that this work might be associated with the general work of the national research council, it was not done in that way in the beginning. I assure the committee that there is no duplication of the work of the national research council.
Where will this be built?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce outlined some of the work. I may have misunderstood him, but I understood the work he planned was going to be along the same lines as that outlined this year and last year by the minister.

No buildings are to be erected out of this vote. This is purely for the payment of salaries and other expenses incidental to the investigational and experimental work. There is nothing for construction.
Are those laboratories government laboratories?

Yes, with the exception of the one in Montreal. The laboratory in Montreal is the result of contributions made by McGill university, by the government and by the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, and each of these bodies is represented on the advisory committee.

National parks bureaul/,0. National parks and historic sites services, $1,261,500.

Two years ago I brought to the attention of the minister an historic 71492-292
site called Watson's Corners, in Lanark county, and at that time he kindly said he would have the matter brought to the attention of the historic sites and monuments board. On June 10, 1937, I received the following letter from the department:
On the 19th of March Mr. Crerar advised you that the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada would consider the suggestion that the site of the old library at Watson's Corners, Lanark county, be fittingly marked.
In the minister's absence, I have received a report from which it appears that the board is of the opinion that this could not be considered as a site of sufficient national importance to warrant the board making a favourable recommendation in the matter.
If I were to take particular note of the letter I really should move that the vote be reduced to one dollar; but I shall not do that this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Thank you.

I shall not do so because of the lateness of the session; but next year I may pursue the matter much farther, because if the site at Watson's Corners is not of national importance, then I want to know what is the national importance of the monument erected up Yonge street in front of one of the golf clubs-I have forgotten which one. I should also like to know the national importance of the monument erected on the height of land between the Mackenzie and Saskatchewan rivers at the old portage. I should like to know the national importance of the site of the monument erected on the town line between the townships of Markham and Scarboro, to the Reesor family. I have made notes of scores and scores of sites, none of which has anything like the historic significance of the site at Watson's Corners. I know that a great many of the sites on which the board has erected monuments are not one-two-three in national importance when compared with the historic library site at Watson's Corners.
Lord Dalhousie was one of the early governors general of Canada, but at first was Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia, and I believe Dalhousie university was created as a result of some of his activities while in that part of Canada. After he became governor general he contributed to and started a library at Quebec city. Later, when he came farther west, he subscribed to one of the first libraries in Ontario-if not the first- which was situated "at Watson's Corners, in the county of Lanark. He was particularly interested in that part of the country because the Scotch settlers who had settled there

Supply-Mines and Resources

had been sent out by the immigration societies of Scotland, following the Napoleonic wars, and had been sent out by the British government, in view of what had happened during the war of 1812, in order to establish a thoroughly loyal community north of the Rideau river. A great many of those settlers came from Lord Dalhousie's estates in Scotland. For that reason one township was called Dalhousie township, and another, Ramsay township, the earl's family name being Ramsay. If any member of the board went out to inspect the Watson's Corners site, I cannot understand why he reported it was not of national importance. I talked to one member of the board who is an educationalist and he told me he knew nothing about it. He was greatly surprised when I told him of the great importance of the site and that it had been turned down as not being of national importance.
Because of the lateness of the hour I shall not take up any more time, but I would ask the minister to look into this matter. When the session is in progress next year I hope there will be more time to discuss this. In my judgment, this is one of the most historic sites in Ontario. It may not be important from a war point of view, but it has great educational significance. In an old building at Watson's Corners are many of the old books which had been donated by Lord Dalhousie in 1828. They are now in an old wooden building. The old library has not been in existence for some time. These books are of historical importance. It was from these books that the early pioneers in that community received their education. Many members of their families have carried all over Canada the learning they obtained from these books. The minister is of Scotch extraction and he will know these Scotch pioneers prized these books. I am thoroughly in earnest when I say that this library site should be looked into.

Following representations which were made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) a year or two ago, this matter was referred specifically to the historic sites and monuments board. I am advised that the practice in the past has been to act only on the recommendation of the board. Naturally many applications are made to the department in connection with particular places that are considered to be of historic importance. As I understand it, the historic sites and monuments board was set up a number of years ago to act in an advisory capacity. Its members are familiar with the general history of the country. I shall be 
happy indeed to bring this matter once more to the attention of the board. Since my hon. friend rose in his place a few moments ago I have been advised that the 'board are to meet in this city early next week. I think it would be quite appropriate if my hon. friend would seek an interview with them and present the claims of this particular site. I would hesitate to act independently of the advice of the board because, if the rule in that regard is once broken, many difficulties will be created. The board is really a sort of buffer between the demands that come from all parts of the country and the administration. It is an independent, non-partisan board and is guided only by a sense of its own responsibilities.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I may be showing my ignorance, but where is Watson's Corners?

In the county of Lanark, in the township of Dalhousie, about six or seven miles from the village of Lanark and about eighteen miles from the town of Perth. It was settled by veterans of the Scotch regiments which fought during the peninsular war under General Ramsay, who later became Lord Dalhousie, and who was made an earl after the battle of Waterloo. These Scotch regiments took a most prominent part in the battle of Waterloo, and following that battle and the war of 1812 they were settled in the township of Dalhousie.

Now that the geography and history lessons are over, I should like to say a few words with reference to a proposed national park in New Brunswick. I think I can truthfully say that New Brunswick is the only province in Canada which has no national park at the present time. While we have a number of historic sites, we have no national park. I am rather ashamed to bring up this matter again because it has been brought up every year since 1936. The minister will remember that in that session a bill was passed authorizing the establishment of national parks in the three maritime provinces. Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia have taken advantage of the provisions of that act and their parks are now being developed.
I understand that the sites of these parks were well selected, and they are proving quite popular with tourists and the people of the provinces.
I should like to see some action taken in New Brunswick. The people of the province are growing weary of the delay, but I do not think the minister is being blamed particularly. I have good reason to believe that the delay is more the responsibility of the

Supply-Mines and Resources
provincial government at Fredericton than it is of the federal government here at Ottawa. Has any definite site been chosen as yet for a national park in New Brunswick? If no definite site has been chosen, what prospective sites have .been reviewed and what is the order of preference? Can the minister give any assurance that the development of a national park in New Brunswick will be undertaken in the near future?
I have not his exact words, but in the session of 1937 the minister intimated that unless the provincial government took some steps to provide for a site, the federal government might have to act in the matter. I do not think it is necessary for me to point out that our province is losing tourist business every year because we have no park. Some $4,000,000 was spent last year for the development of parks throughout Canada, tout not one dollar of that was spent in New Brunswick. The fact that our province is beautiful is self-evident to anyone who visits it. We have splendid roads, and I believe that if a park were established it would prove a great added attraction so far as tourist trade is concerned.
There is another matter in connection with which the province is losing. I refer to relief projects. I understand that between $600,000 and $700,000 has 'been spent for relief purposes in developing the Nova Scotia site. I have heard considerable criticism of the way in which this money has been used, but we in New Brunswick feel that the federal government and the provincial government should endeavour to get together on this matter and provide a national park for our province. I should like to have some comment from the minister in this regard.

Up to the present time no site has been selected for a national park in New Brunswick. My hon. friend is in error when he says that according to his memory I stated in the house a year or two years ago that if the provincial government did not act the federal government would.
The minister intimated that he was growing impatient.

I do not wish the committee to get any wrong impression. I have stated several times when the parks votes have been under consideration in the past that the provincial authority has first to acquire the area and deed it over to the federal administration.
I think that is generally understood.

There are several sites in New Brunswick, perhaps of varying degrees of suitability, any one of which would be a 71492-2921
good park site; but I understand the provincial government, which has to provide the area free to the parks administration, finds itself in the position where it has to acquire considerable private property. We will not take over a park area if private property is held within its boundaries because we want complete control, which is necessary if we are to develop the area suitably for park purposes. I can assure my hon. friend that so far as the federal administration is concerned, we shall be prepared to go ahead when we secure the area; or rather I will put it in this way:
I am prepared to recommend to the government the commencement of development work on such a park site once the area is selected. At the same time I am bound to say that I recognize the difficulties which the provincial government have to overcome in getting an area. If they were starting de novo in an area where there was no settlement it would be a comparatively easy matter. That was the situation not only in connection with the Cape Breton Highlands park site in Nova Scotia, but very largely in Prince Edward Island.
They surmounted the difficulties.

They surmounted the difficulties, but the difficulties were not nearly so great as I understand they are in New Brunswick. That is the position. I know the matter has been engaging the attention of the provincial government, and possibly by another year we shall be able to make a definite start.

The minister did not answer one question I asked with reference to the survey that has been made by his department and as to whether there was any order of preference in the sites surveyed-first choice, second choice, third choice, et cetera. My opinion. I might state to the minister, is that the difficulty is not so much in obtaining the land as local jealousy in different parts of the province, and the provincial government does not seem to have the back-bone to go ahead and make a decision.

If there are such difficulties I know nothing of them, but I do know enough of the situation to be quite certain of what I said a moment ago that there are difficulties in the way of securing the necessary area. I cannot recall at the moment the order of preference, and I am sorry I have not the information here. Various sites suggested have been examined by competent parks officials, men who have done that work in the other provinces. They furnish maps and complete detailed information regarding the different areas. I believe they did classify
Supply-Mines and Resources

the areas in order of preference according to their judgment. I have not that information here tonight, but I can give it to my hon. friend if he desires to have it.
I should be glad if the minister would supply me with the information.

I should like to draw to the attention of the minister a matter affecting the employment conditions of some men who work in the Clear Lake national park in Manitoba. I have been asked to do so by a certain organization in Winnipeg. While these men are not employees of the government, they work as musicians for a man who has a dance-hall concession in the Clear Lake park. He is their employer, and there has been a dispute between the concessionnaire and the men he employs as musicians. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) and I have had communications from the city of Winnipeg in reference to conditions of employment there. This man has a monopoly of the concessions there from the parks branch. While I am not personally familiar with the situation beyond what I have learned from communications received, I must say that there seems to be something in the complaint of the Winnipeg musicians' organization, which has taken this matter up on behalf of the musicians working at the dance hall in the park. From correspondence we have had with this organization, it appears that these musicians are employed seven days a week at a salary of fifteen dollars a week.

If my hon. friend will permit me to say a word, I do not think it will be necessary for him to labour the point. The matter has been drawn to the attention of the department. This concession was secured several years ago. It was granted not by the present government but by the previous administration. There is an annual licence fee charged, and in the licence issued this year a provision was inserted that the licencee must pay the scale of wages approved by the province for that class of employees. I hope that will overcome the difficulty mentioned by my hon. friend.

While I do not want to
labour the point at any length, I do not know whether the provincial government have set up any scale of pay for musicians. They may have schedules applying to other classes of work, but I doubt very much whether there is such a thing as an approved scale of pay by the province for musicians working in any part of Manitoba. But if an annual licence is granted by the department, there would

be a means of seeing that the men employed as musicians receive at least decent remuneration for the services they render. I draw the matter to the attention of the minister this evening, and if necessary I can take it up with the department later if the grievances are not properly adjusted.

We have been advised
that rates of pay will be established by the provincial department of labour covering the employees engaged in this particular dance hall. I do not think we can go beyond that. The question of what the operator of this hall shall pay to his employees is not, as my hon. friend knows, a question over which the federal government has control.

I cannot allow that statement to go unchallenged. If that were to be accepted, it would be establishing a bad principle. At the present time the federal government in its own contracts always inserts some kind of a fair-wage clause. In this instance we are not exactly letting a contract but are giving a lease to some person who is using it for purposes of gain. I am sorry that I could not accept the statement of the minister, but no doubt we shall hear a little more about the matter at a later date, and we can see how it works out in the present year.
I think it will be remedied.
Has the minister received any recent request from the government of British Columbia to take over the Garibaldi area as a national park?

I understand that the
matter was brought to our attention some time ago-I am not in a position to say at the moment how long ago it was-by the British Columbia government.

152. International Boundary Commission, $30,800.
How many members are there on this commission, and who are the Canadian members?

We have one representative on this International Boundary Commission, and he has a small staff. This has to do largely with the maintenance of the markers on the boundary and the settlement of questions relating to the international boundary. In some instances, where the boundary line passes through areas which have been forested, the line between the two countries has been cleared for a certain width. In certain places that requires some attention every year. There are other parts where the monuments which are set up at stated intervals to indicate the boundary line have to be restored or renewed. This commission is an international commission in the sense that the United States have a representative on it, and these two representatives are the ones who carry on this work.
Who is the Canadian representative?
Mr. N. J. Ogilvie.
